name: Matter and Materials
what_is_it: Matter and Materials studies what everything around us is made of, how particles behave in solids, liquids and gases, and how substances can change physically and chemically.
why_it_matters: Understanding matter explains everyday phenomena — why ice melts, why steam rises, why mixing chemicals in a kitchen can be dangerous — and underpins chemistry, engineering, cooking, and materials science.
key_vocabulary: Matter — anything that has mass and takes up space (volume)
Particle — a tiny piece of matter (atom or molecule) too small to see individually
Solid — matter with a fixed shape and fixed volume; particles vibrate in place, tightly packed
Liquid — matter with a fixed volume but no fixed shape; particles are close but can slide past each other
Gas — matter with no fixed shape or volume; particles are far apart and move freely
Physical change — a change that alters the form of a substance without creating a new substance (e.g. melting)
Chemical change — a change that produces a new substance with different properties (e.g. burning, rusting)
Mixture — two or more substances combined without chemically bonding, so each keeps its own properties
Pure substance — a substance made of only one kind of particle (an element or a compound)
core_concept: All matter is made of tiny moving particles. How closely packed and how freely those particles move determines whether a substance is a solid, liquid, or gas — and heating or cooling matter changes how much the particles move, which is why substances change state.
key_facts: Heating a solid gives its particles more energy, making them vibrate more until they break free into a liquid (melting).
Heating a liquid enough gives particles so much energy they escape into a gas (boiling/evaporation).
Cooling a gas causes particles to slow down and come together into a liquid (condensation), and cooling a liquid further can form a solid (freezing).
In a physical change (like melting or dissolving), no new substance is formed and the change can usually be reversed.
In a chemical change (like burning or rusting), a new substance with new properties is formed and it is usually difficult to reverse.
Mixtures can be separated using physical methods (filtration, evaporation, sieving) because the substances haven't chemically combined.
common_misconceptions: Thinking particles themselves expand when heated — actually the particles move FASTER and spread further apart, they don't get bigger.
Believing gas has no mass — gases have mass, just spread out over a larger volume.
Assuming all mixtures look mixed — a solution (like sugar in water) is a mixture even though you can't see separate parts.
Confusing melting (solid→liquid) with dissolving (a solid spreading through a liquid) — these are different processes.
